analysis.one_liner: Bans new oil, gas, and mining development on federal land around Chaco Canyon, New Mexico.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Energy Committee despite an August 2018 hearing; the 115th Congress ended with no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently bar new leasing and mining on federal land within the Chaco Cultural Heritage Withdrawal Area in New Mexico, keeping new oil and gas drilling and hardrock mining out of the landscape around Chaco Culture National Historical Park. Existing leases and rights would continue, and tribal mineral rights would not be affected. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, got a subcommittee hearing in August 2018, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the Navajo communities surrounding the Greater Chaco region, who have lived with drilling next to homes, schools, and ceremonial sites, and the general public, who gain permanent protection of a World Heritage cultural landscape from new industrial development.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Navajo communities near Chaco and public-lands users

how_it_helps.text: The bill withdraws federal land in the Chaco Cultural Heritage Withdrawal Area from entry, disposal, mining claims, and operation of the mineral leasing, mineral materials, and geothermal leasing laws, blocking new oil, gas, and mining development in the area.
The withdrawal also applies to any land the federal government acquires within the area after enactment, so the protection cannot be eroded by land trades.

The bill leaves untouched the mineral rights of a Tribe or tribal member on trust or allotment land, and preserves valid existing rights, so it protects cultural sites without stripping anyone's current legal interests.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and mining companies lose the opportunity to lease and develop federal minerals in the withdrawal area. The federal government and New Mexico forgo potential royalty revenue from those unleased minerals.

drawbacks.text: The bill locks up federal minerals in a natural-gas-rich basin, forgoing royalty revenue that funds federal, state, and tribal budgets.
It does not restrict development on existing leases held under valid existing rights, so new drilling could continue on lands already leased even while new leasing is barred.

Restricting federal drilling can shift production to private or state lands nearby, which would give opponents' health and environmental concerns little relief if activity moves just outside the withdrawal boundary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection addresses a well-documented local concern — drilling expanding toward homes and an internationally significant archaeological site — at the cost of forgone future mineral revenue on a small slice of federal land. The main design weakness is that valid existing leases continue, so the relief for nearby residents is partial rather than complete.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and received a subcommittee hearing in August 2018, but the committee never voted on it and it never reached the Senate floor before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Udall introduced the bill with Senator Martin Heinrich as cosponsor on May 22, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The committee's Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining held a hearing on the bill on August 22, 2018.
No further action was taken; the bill received no committee vote and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and mining interests are better off because the bill died: new leasing and development of federal minerals in the Chaco withdrawal area remained possible. Residents near the park gained nothing from this bill, though the 115th Congress's end left the question open for a later Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, and mining developers kept access

for.name: Sen. Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Chaco Cultural Heritage Area Protection Act and shepherded it to a subcommittee hearing.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing on the bill on August 22, 2018 but never scheduled a committee vote, so the bill never reached the floor.

against.name: Oil and gas producers in the San Juan Basin
against.role: Holders of and bidders on federal mineral leases around Greater Chaco
against.what_they_did: Opposed withdrawal of federal minerals around Chaco from leasing, which would remove acreage from future development.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded. Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough to reveal whether it had broader bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Oil and gas developers (San Juan Basin / Greater Chaco region)
industries.note: The bill removes federal minerals in the withdrawal area from new leasing under the mineral leasing laws, foreclosing future drilling acreage in a productive gas basin. Residents near the park have pushed back against drilling expanding toward homes and the cultural site, so the industry's gain from continued access runs against the bill's beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining and mineral materials operators
industries.note: The bill withdraws the land from location, entry, and patent under mining laws and from mineral materials disposal, closing it to new mining claims. This is a smaller interest than oil and gas but faces the same closed door.
